messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Vignette:
Thomas, a 49-year-old City Council Member, sits rigidly in the chair, his gaze fixed somewhere beyond the wall, occasionally darting to the door. He recounts the incident that brought him here, haltingly at first, as if picking through broken glass. He was deployed overseas, a lifetime ago it feels, when their convoy was ambushed. He remembers the sudden, deafening roar, the immediate impact, and then a chaotic blur of dust, shouts, and gunfire. He tries to explain the sequence of events, but the details are fragmented; certain moments are sharp, almost painfully vivid, while others are entirely missing, leaving large, unsettling gaps. When he attempts to connect these pieces, the narrative unravels, and he loses his train of thought, unable to finish a sentence. It’s not just the words that fail him; trying to piece it together brings back the same visceral terror he felt at the time, a gripping fear that makes his chest tighten and his breath catch.

After returning home, the world felt fundamentally altered. He had come to believe, with an unshakable certainty, that the world was a dangerous place, a belief reinforced by every sudden noise or unexpected movement. His body, he felt, had betrayed him, constantly reacting as if he were still in the thick of combat, even when he was safe in his own home. He was always on guard, his senses heightened, scanning every room he entered, every crowd he navigated. This relentless hypervigilance left him utterly exhausted. He struggled to fall asleep, his mind racing, and if he did drift off, he would often wake abruptly, his heart pounding.

His public role as a City Council Member, which once energized him, had become a minefield. At town hall meetings or community events, a well-meaning constituent might place a hand on his arm or back, and he would flinch violently, reacting with alarm to the unexpected contact. He found it impossible to trust assurances of safety, even from his wife, Sarah, or his closest colleagues; the internal alarm bells were always ringing. To cope, Thomas had developed a series of habits. When driving home from a particularly stressful council meeting, he would blast loud music, or keep the television on constantly at home, the noise a shield against the silence that allowed his thoughts to spiral. What frightened him most was the persistent feeling that he was losing his mind; he found himself constantly monitoring his own thoughts, searching for any sign that he was truly "going crazy" because of his body's uncontrollable reactions.

The most challenging aspect, both professionally and personally, was his inability to tolerate physical contact. Handshakes at public events became an agonizing ordeal he tried to avoid, often crossing his arms or keeping his distance. At home, his marriage to Sarah, once close and physically affectionate, had grown distant. He found himself stiffening whenever she tried to touch him, creating a chasm between them that he didn't know how to bridge. This growing isolation, combined with the relentless internal siege and the fear that he was losing himself, finally prompted him to seek help. He worried that if he continued down this path, he would completely alienate everyone he cared about, and lose the sense of purpose he once found in his work.
